A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Memento No More study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original ToolQA experiments, held-out-template evaluation, coding and reasoning benchmark results, and a cross-entropy training comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds OfficeBench evaluations, component ablations, and further benchmark and efficiency measurements.

M1.justification: The ReAct/Python architecture, iterative hint distillation, LoRA updates, probabilistic hint dropout, and data balancing are already present in v1. v2 specifies forward KL and additional implementation details, but does not establish a new algorithmic component. OfficeBench applies the existing procedure to another task domain.

E1.justification: v2 adds training and evaluation on 286 OfficeBench tasks spanning six applications and workflows requiring one to three applications. These non-templated document, spreadsheet, email, and calendar workflows substantially extend coverage beyond ToolQA. The six ToolQA groups and HumanEval/GSM8K evaluations remain.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain the Llama-3.1-70B prompt baselines, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, and cross-entropy training on successful trajectories. OfficeBench extends the same comparator set to another benchmark. The new dropout and balancing experiments vary components of MNM rather than introduce separate baseline methods.

E3.justification: OfficeBench introduces a 67/3/30 training/validation/test split and its own training schedule, including four teacher trajectories per task and seven epochs in Round 1. New ablations vary dropout and balancing. Existing ToolQA descriptions also change: filter counts become 15/21 instead of 14/18, and held-out templates are described as a three-way 60/10/30 split rather than a shared training/validation template pool plus test templates. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix C.3 adds direct tests of two previously unablated components: dropout rates 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, and 1.0, and training with versus without data balancing, on both benchmarks. Coding and reasoning skill-retention checks also cover OfficeBench-trained agents. The earlier held-out-template and cross-entropy analyses are retained.

E5.justification: For held-out ToolQA tasks, v1 reports one DeepSeek-V3 trial without uncertainty, whereas v2 reports three trials and adds standard errors (v1 Table 4; v2 Table 5). The general mean-and-standard-error reporting practice remains, and GPT-4o remains a single-trial comparison.

E6.justification: New OfficeBench results include Round 3 MNM success of 90.3%, compared with GPT-4o at 89.9% and DeepSeek-V3 at 86.9%. v2 also adds ablation results, OfficeBench token counts, and skill-retention scores. The headline ToolQA results remain unchanged. Held-out DeepSeek-V3 entries are revised under three-trial reporting, such as Yelp changing from a single-trial 78.2% to a mean of 84.9%; this is not a demonstrated same-setting model improvement.

T1.justification: The state and policy definitions, LoRA update equations, and Algorithm 1 are substantively retained. v2 explicitly states the direction of the existing KL objective but adds no new derivation, theorem, or proof. Its new applicability conditions are qualitative limitations rather than formal theoretical assumptions.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains iterative internalization of human hints without requiring expert demonstrations. The abstract and conclusion extend the explicit empirical outperformance claim from ToolQA to ToolQA and OfficeBench, including the new 90.3% OfficeBench result, without redefining the methodological contribution.

C2.justification: New Section 6 and Appendix A discuss human-supervision scalability, annotator expertise, required overlap in tool usage, training-time tool information, and reliance on ground-truth checks to identify failures. They explicitly acknowledge that cross-domain sequential training was not tested. Appendix C.3 also adds explanations of dropout through attention preservation, data augmentation, and easier hint internalization.

D1.justification: v2 adds extensive initial and corrective hint listings, OfficeBench tool and preprocessing documentation, reviewer-model identity, LoRA precision/layer coverage/merging details, and hardware and training times. A first-page footnote newly states that code and checkpoints are available. Much existing training information is relocated to Appendix E; exact ToolQA split counts and the explicit exact-string-match description from v1 are omitted.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Lost in the Middle, CLIN, AVATAR, OfficeBench, Pomerleau, and Sarch et al. It adds a substantive distinction from Sarch et al.'s abstraction-level feedback for vision-language agents. The related-work organization and claimed novelty of extending context distillation to interactive LLM agents remain.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized around two benchmarks, with detailed training descriptions moved from Section 5.3 into Appendix E. v2 introduces a main discussion section and reorganizes the appendices around limitations, results, efficiency, training, tools, preprocessing, and hints. Existing task examples and broader-impact material are relocated, while much introductory and methodological prose is retained.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from two columns to one, substantially reflows figures and tables, and displays the prompt structure as a numbered listing beside Figure 2. It adds OfficeBench and ablation tables, expands the existing coding/reasoning and token-usage tables, and introduces extensive formatted hint listings. Figures 1–4 are retained rather than replaced by new scientific figures.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's ToolQA-centered evidence through distinct OfficeBench workflows and ablations of two important components. Detailed hints, implementation disclosures, and explicit applicability limitations materially improve reproducibility and interpretation. Some reporting weaknesses remain: the OfficeBench advantage over GPT-4o is narrow, and Table 9 implies approximately 14–17% of baseline input-token usage, inconsistent with the stated 7–10%. The broader validation and improved transparency outweigh these limitations; the improvement does not depend on the unchanged headline ToolQA scores.
